title: Wise attention
hookLine: don't ask "did I exist in the past"; ask "what is dukkha, what ends it" (MN 2)

lines: WHO AM I? WHAT WAS I?
cards: Three in the morning, and the questions start. Who am I, really? What was I before all this?
Will any of it matter? What if I've got everything wrong? You can turn those over for hours and get up more tired than you lay down.
In an old discourse, the Buddha listed nearly the same questions, almost one for one. Then he said something surprising about them.

teach.h: WAS I? AM I? WHAT AM I?
teach.b: In MN 2, the first way with the taints is seeing, and seeing depends on how you attend. Unwise attention comes first. A person wonders: Was I in the past?
Was I not? What was I? Will I be in the future?
What will I be? And now: Am I? Am I not?
What am I? Where did this being come from, and where will it go? Then they settle on a view.
I have a self. Or, I have no self. Or some other.
The Buddha calls all of these a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a fetter of views. Notice that even I have no self is on that list, as a view to get tangled in.
He doesn't call the people who ask foolish; he calls these questions unfit for attention. Then wise attention, yoniso manasikara. Manasikara is attention, literally making in the mind.
Yoniso comes from yoni, a womb, a source: attention that goes back to where things come from.

teach.h: WHAT IS DUKKHA? WHAT ENDS IT?
teach.b: And it attends to this: this is dukkha; this is its arising; this is its ending; this is the way to its ending. The four noble truths, used as questions.
A useful question changes something: where is the suffering in this, what's feeding it, what would ease it?
And the text says attention like this cuts three fetters: the view of a fixed self, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals. Not a small result, for changing what you ask.

how: Teachers in many Buddhist schools emphasize wise attention, yoniso manasikara, as the ground of practice; Theravada teachers often present the four noble truths as a way of looking at any experience.

o: careful focus on one object for a long time
thinking hard about who you really are
attention that traces things back to their source

games.q: match the words of wise attention.
p: what is dukkha, what ends it

s: the Buddha calls the big questions about the self foolish
he calls them unfit for attention: they lead into a thicket of views, not out of dukkha.
in MN 2, even 'I have no self' is listed among the views
it's one of the views unwise attention settles on.
wise attention cuts three fetters, the text says
the view of a fixed self, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals.

games.q: it's 3 a.m. and you're asking: what was I in the past? what does MN 2 suggest?
o: keep thinking until you find the answer
ask instead: what is dukkha here, and what ends it?
decide you have no self and go back to sleep
games.why: MN 2 turns attention to the four truths: this is dukkha, its arising, its ending, the way. even 'I have no self' is listed as a view to get stuck in.

practice: Find a question that's been circling lately, like why does this always happen to me, and hold it for a breath. Then turn it toward right now: where is the tension in the body, what's feeding it, what would ease it, even a little?
No answers needed; just notice whether the new question sits differently.

wordCard.voice: Wise attention. Yoniso manasikara: attention that goes back to the source, and asks what is suffering and what ends it.

orig.note: Pali yoniso manasikāra: wise attention, attention by way of the source.

carryVoice: Your line: the useful question. It asks what would ease this, not who you really are. That's day four hundred four.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 2, Sabbasava Sutta (taints abandoned by seeing)
